abstract: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0 (July 23, 2026) — an ongoing economic research initiative from Google and Google DeepMind (Iscenko, Strand, Chen, Imas, Manyika et al., with review by Diane Coyle and David Autor). Analyzes 15 million de-identified interactions across the Gemini App, Google AI Mode, and Gemini API (April 6-19, 2026), mapped via privacy-preserving clustering (OCTO) to 800+ occupations, 4,000 O*NET tasks, 300 ATUS household activities, 150 countries, and 140 languages. Completes the usage-data triad alongside the Anthropic Economic Index and OpenAI's Jobs Transition Framework, and uniquely adds household time-use (ATUS) and multilingual lenses. Headline: diffusion is very broad but shallow — usage spans occupations covering 88% of US employment, yet the median occupation with any use applies AI to only 21% of its tasks, and end-to-end automation is rare.
keyFindings: Gemini use observed in 68% of detailed occupations, collectively representing 88.4% of US civilian employment — but 'penetration remains shallow and overwhelmingly collaborative'
Median task saturation is 21% among occupations with any AI use; only 3% of occupations show usage across >75% of their tasks; 29% of occupations show zero task saturation

End-to-end task automation represents <10% of AI conversations in non-routine cognitive work; >25% for routine cognitive work — most usage is Partial Drafting, Review/Refinement, Ideation, or Information Retrieval
Non-routine cognitive tasks are 35% of the O*NET task universe but 65% of work-related Gemini interactions — a discontinuity with prior routine-biased technological change

Wage gradient: a 1% increase in an occupation's median earnings is associated with >2.5% higher AI usage intensity; Gemini-conversation-weighted median salary is $82,919 vs the $62,252 employment-weighted national median
AI is not white-collar-only: automotive technicians and industrial mechanics use multimodal AI (2x baseline rate) for diagnostics, troubleshooting, and inspection
Usage is over-represented in LOW-expertise non-routine cognitive tasks despite high-earning workers adopting at the highest rates — a complex expertise-usage relationship
86% of conversational AI use occurs outside work; household time-savings valued at $14.9B (0.5% scenario) to $149B (5% scenario) annually in the US, invisible to GDP
Government services & civic obligations are over-represented ~20x vs actual time spent; nearly half of medical/legal/financial/government AI consultations occur outside 9-to-5 hours
Global: 1% higher GDP per capita → 0.9% more AI usage; lowest-adopting country quintile holds 17% of world population but generates 2% of conversations
English is only ~1/3 of global conversations across 143 languages; work and non-work language distributions are nearly identical — no evidence users abandon native languages for professional tasks
Explicitly does NOT find support for imminent mass white-collar automation, AI irrelevance to blue-collar work, or a strictly US-China adoption race
methodology: Privacy-preserving automated pipeline: 14,653,926 de-identified interactions sampled April 6-19, 2026 across three surfaces (~5M each). PII stripped via DLP filters; conversations classified work/non-work (93.7% accuracy on synthetic validation), summarized, clustered via Google DeepMind's OCTO tool, and mapped to BLS SOC/O*NET (work) and ATUS (non-work) taxonomies. K-anonymization discards clusters under 10 unique users. Classifier validation: 71.6% accuracy at SOC major-group level (vs 4.4% random), 22.6% at exact O*NET task level (4,244x lift over random), 70.4% agreement at Autor-Thompson task-type level; human raters judged 86-98% of labels 'reasonable' depending on granularity. Autor-Thompson (2025) expertise and task-type frameworks applied throughout.
qualifiers: Excludes paid Gemini API (enterprise) usage, Google Workspace, AI Overviews, and Translate — enterprise professional use cases likely under-represented. Measures behavioral interactions, not productivity outcomes: a conversation doesn't guarantee the user accomplished anything. Captures current usage, not potential impact; non-adopters invisible. Classifications are probabilistic — granular occupation/task findings carry more uncertainty than major-group trends. Sample window (Apr 6-19) overlaps US tax season, likely inflating tax-adjacent occupations. Authors explicitly state ATLAS v1.0 cannot yet address whether AI dampens entry-level hiring or deepens the digital divide. Intent and expertise classifiers are first-iteration. The 88% employment-coverage figure uses a weak threshold (≥50 users globally per occupation) — it measures diffusion breadth, not exposure depth.
